Family Health

Haemorrhoids or bowel cancer: why overlapping symptoms need checking

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Haemorrhoids commonly cause anal symptoms, but bleeding and a lump should not be diagnosed by appearance alone. Understanding the overlap can help you seek the right assessment without assuming the worst or overlooking a persistent change.

Similar symptoms do not mean the same condition

Seeing blood after a bowel movement or finding a lump near the anus can be alarming. Haemorrhoids, also called piles, are a common explanation, but symptoms alone cannot show whether they are the cause. A previous diagnosis of piles also does not explain every new episode automatically.

Haemorrhoids are enlarged vascular cushions in or around the anal canal. Colorectal cancer starts in the colon or rectum. Anal cancer is a separate cancer affecting the anal region. These conditions can overlap in their symptoms even though they arise in different tissues and need different care.

Haemorrhoids do not turn into colorectal cancer. It is possible, however, to have haemorrhoids and another bowel condition at the same time. The useful response to bleeding is neither to assume cancer nor to dismiss it, but to arrange an assessment that fits the symptoms and their severity.

Rectal bleeding needs an explanation

Blood may appear on toilet paper, drip into the bowl, coat a stool or seem mixed through it. Internal haemorrhoids can cause bright red bleeding, often without pain. Cancer, inflammation, fissures and other problems can also bleed, so this appearance is not proof of piles.

Colour can provide a clue, but it does not reliably locate the source by itself. Bright red blood can come from the lower bowel, while black, tarry stool may indicate bleeding higher in the digestive tract. Dark red blood is not a dependable sign that the small bowel is responsible.

Tell the clinician what you actually noticed, including the amount, frequency and whether the stool itself changed. Mention medicines such as iron, bismuth or blood thinners, because they can affect appearance or bleeding risk. Do not stop a prescribed blood thinner independently, and do not use a change in stool colour alone to decide that an episode is harmless.

Itching and lumps also have several explanations

Moisture, mucus, small amounts of stool and repeated wiping can irritate the skin around the anus. Itching may accompany piles, but it is not specific to them or to cancer. Scrubbing harder can worsen irritated skin rather than solve the underlying problem.

An external haemorrhoid can form a lump near the opening. An internal haemorrhoid that slips outward, called a prolapse, can also be felt there. A clot in an external haemorrhoid may produce a particularly tender, firm lump; this is called a thrombosed haemorrhoid.

A new lump, persistent sore or changing area should be examined instead of repeatedly treated as piles. Anal cancer and other conditions can affect this region, while a lump at the opening is not the usual way a cancer farther up the colon is detected. Location is helpful information, not a diagnosis to make by touch at home.

Notice changes in your usual bowel pattern

A bowel change means something different from your own normal pattern. It may involve persistent diarrhoea, constipation, a change in stool shape, blood or mucus, or needing to go more or less often. One unusually narrow stool does not establish cancer, but a persistent change deserves discussion.

Another symptom is feeling that you still need to pass stool after going, sometimes with straining or discomfort. This is often called tenesmus. It can occur with rectal disease, including inflammation or cancer, and cannot be attributed to haemorrhoids solely because piles are also present.

Keep a brief record of when the change started and whether it is ongoing or intermittent. Avoid judging the pattern from one day or comparing your bowel frequency with someone else’s. Explain any associated pain, discharge or urgency, because the combination can help the clinician decide what to investigate.

Abdominal symptoms, weight loss and tiredness matter

Persistent abdominal cramping, bloating or discomfort needs consideration beyond a local anal problem. Haemorrhoids do not ordinarily explain ongoing abdominal symptoms. Constipation or another bowel condition may coexist, so several symptoms do not necessarily have one cause.

Unintentional weight loss also deserves assessment. There is no useful single percentage that predicts how many people with colorectal cancer will experience it, or how much weight loss proves a diagnosis. Do not wait for weight loss to appear before asking about bleeding.

Blood loss over time can lead to anaemia and contribute to weakness, fatigue or shortness of breath. Sometimes bleeding is not visible. A blood count can be useful when indicated, but tiredness has many possible explanations. The aim is to investigate the cause of symptoms rather than regard them as a cancer checklist.

Pain does not reliably distinguish piles from cancer

Uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids are often painless. A prolapsed haemorrhoid can be uncomfortable, and an external haemorrhoid containing a clot can be very painful. It is therefore inaccurate to assume that rectal pain is usually caused by internal piles.

Fissures, abscesses, inflammation and other problems can also cause anal or rectal pain. Colorectal cancer may have no symptoms early on, and the presence or absence of pain does not rule it in or out. Severe pain should not be used as a reason to choose a home diagnosis.

Seek prompt care for marked or worsening pain, especially with fever, swelling or discharge. If a lump is suddenly very painful, a clinician can assess whether a thrombosed haemorrhoid or another condition needs treatment. Do not cut, puncture or attempt to drain it yourself.

Know when bleeding needs urgent help

Get emergency help if bleeding does not stop or there is a large amount of blood, such as red toilet water or large clots. Fainting, severe dizziness, collapse, chest pain or difficulty breathing alongside bleeding also needs emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself if you feel faint or unwell.

Black or dark red stool, bloody diarrhoea or significant worsening symptoms require urgent medical advice. A small first episode may have a less serious cause, but new, recurrent or unexplained rectal bleeding should still be discussed with a clinician. Persistent anal symptoms despite home care also need review.

Do not wait until a routine screening age or assume that being under forty excludes bowel cancer. Screening is intended for people without symptoms; investigating symptoms is a different task. Tell the team if you have a family history of bowel cancer, previous polyps, inflammatory bowel disease or another relevant condition.

What an assessment can and cannot establish

The clinician asks about bleeding, bowel habits, pain, weight changes, medicines and personal or family history. They may inspect the anal area and perform a gloved finger examination of the rectum. You can ask for an explanation, a chaperone and a pause if the examination is painful.

Finding haemorrhoids can explain some symptoms, but a brief examination does not inspect the whole colon or automatically exclude another disease. Depending on the findings and local pathway, further checks may include blood tests, a stool test or an examination of more of the bowel, such as colonoscopy.

Ask what the working explanation is, which tests are needed and what should happen if symptoms continue. Not everyone needs the same investigation, but there should be a follow-up plan. Report ongoing bleeding or new symptoms even if the first examination or test was reassuring.

Home care can help when haemorrhoids are confirmed

Aim for soft, easy-to-pass stools with fibre-rich foods and appropriate fluids. Increase fibre gradually if it causes bloating, and follow any medical fluid restriction. Avoid straining, prolonged sitting on the toilet and repeatedly delaying a bowel movement.

A comfortably warm bath may ease soreness. A wrapped cold pack can help swelling for short periods; keep ice off bare skin. Clean gently and pat dry rather than scrub. Ask a pharmacist about short-term creams, ointments or suppositories and follow their directions, especially during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Paracetamol may be an option for pain when suitable. NHS advice is to avoid ibuprofen if piles are bleeding and to avoid codeine-containing painkillers because constipation can worsen symptoms. Symptom relief does not remove the need to investigate unexplained bleeding or reassess symptoms that persist.

Procedures depend on the type and severity of piles

Persistent bleeding, troublesome prolapse or a painful thrombosed haemorrhoid may need more than home care. Options for selected internal piles include rubber-band ligation, injections or other office treatments. Some people need an operation to remove or reposition haemorrhoidal tissue.

These are not all equivalent minor procedures without anaesthesia. The choice, pain relief, recovery and risks depend on the actual treatment and your health. A clinician may consider a procedure for an acutely painful external clot, but it should never be drained at home.

Ask how the treatment is expected to help, how recurrence is managed and which symptoms afterward require a call. Continue the bowel-habit plan as advised. If bleeding changes, returns or is accompanied by new bowel or general symptoms, seek reassessment rather than assuming the original diagnosis covers everything.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Internal piles often bleed without pain.

Blood colour or a finding of piles does not exclude another bowel condition.

Persistent or unexplained symptoms need assessment regardless of screening age.

How BeMama can help

Write down when symptoms began, what the bleeding looks like, any bowel changes and the medicines you take, then agree on a clear follow-up plan.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for nonstop or large-volume bleeding, large clots, fainting or severe illness. Black or dark red stool and bloody diarrhoea need urgent medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Haemorrhoids do not turn into bowel cancer.
  • Several conditions can cause itching, lumps or rectal bleeding.
  • Pain is not a reliable way to distinguish the cause.
  • A brief rectal examination does not inspect the whole bowel.
  • New or persistent symptoms deserve reassessment.

Frequently asked questions

Do haemorrhoids turn into colorectal cancer?

No. They are different conditions, although a person can have piles and another bowel problem at the same time.

Does bright red blood prove I have piles?

No. Other conditions, including cancer and inflammation, can also cause bright red bleeding.

Are internal piles always painful?

No. Uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids are often painless; prolapse or an external clot can cause pain.

Can a clot in a pile make a hard lump?

Yes. A thrombosed external haemorrhoid can be firm and tender, but a new painful lump needs assessment.

Does a narrow stool mean cancer?

Not by itself. A persistent change from your normal bowel pattern should be discussed with a clinician.

Should I wait until I am old enough for screening?

No. Assessment of symptoms is different from routine screening and may be needed at any age.

Does finding piles rule out cancer elsewhere?

No. A local examination does not inspect the whole colon, and further tests may be appropriate.

Can I take ibuprofen for bleeding piles?

NHS advice is to avoid ibuprofen when piles are bleeding. Ask about suitable pain relief and do not stop prescribed medicines without advice.

Are all haemorrhoid procedures done without anaesthesia?

No. Office procedures and operations differ in preparation, pain relief and recovery.

Which bleeding needs emergency help?

Bleeding that will not stop, a large amount of blood or clots, or bleeding with fainting, severe dizziness or serious illness needs emergency assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
